overview: The Kushans, a Yuezhi clan from Bactria, built an empire from the Oxus to the Ganges in the first three centuries CE. They struck gold coins, stood at the crossing of the Silk Road, and under Kanishka became the great patrons of Buddhism and the art of Gandhara.

items.text: Gandharan sculptors, drawing on Greek and Roman models, made some of the first images of the Buddha in human form, at the same time as the workshops of Mathura.
Stupas and monasteries rose at Taxila, Peshawar and Hadda; Chinese pilgrims reported Kanishka's stupa at Peshawar as the tallest building they had seen.
The empire held the passes between the Silk Road, the Indus ports and the Ganges plain, and traded with Rome by sea and with Han China by land.
Gold coins on the Roman weight standard, showing Greek, Iranian, Indian and Buddhist gods, circulated from Central Asia to the Ganges.
Kanishka's reign, beginning about 127 CE, is remembered in Buddhist tradition for a council in Kashmir that fixed the canon of the Sarvastivada school.
Zoroastrian, Greek, Hindu and Buddhist deities all appear on Kushan coins, and Bactrian, written in Greek letters, was the language of the state.
Gandharan Buddhist art traveled along the Silk Road to Central Asia and China.
Kushan patronage helped carry Buddhism to Central Asia and on to China.

fall.text: The Sasanians took Bactria and the west in the third century and set up Kushano-Sasanian governors; the last Kushan kings ruled in the Punjab in the shadow of the Guptas until about 375.
